Indexes.summary: Indexes are auxiliary structures (often B-trees) that speed lookups, sorts, and joins at write/storage cost.
Indexes.problem: Without them, planners fall back to sequential scans that worsen as tables grow.
Indexes.mechanics: CREATE INDEX builds a sorted structure; planner chooses index vs seq scan using stats.
Indexes.tradeoffs: Too many indexes slow writes. Partial/expression indexes target narrow workloads.
Indexes.troubleshoot: Seq scans on selective filters: missing/wrong index—EXPLAIN ANALYZE and check usage stats.
Indexes.example: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_created ON orders(user_id, created_at DESC);
Indexes.integration: 1) Index FK/filter/sort columns. 2) EXPLAIN slow queries. 3) Drop unused. 4) Create concurrently in prod.

B-tree index.summary: B-tree indexes keep keys in sorted balanced trees—Postgres’s default for equality and range predicates.
B-tree index.problem: They accelerate WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY on sortable types.
B-tree index.mechanics: Lookups descend to leaf pages; range scans walk leaves. Multicolumn (a,b) supports a and a+b, not b alone.
B-tree index.tradeoffs: Hash is narrower; GIN/GiST for composites/docs. B-trees can bloat—VACUUM/REINDEX when needed.
B-tree index.troubleshoot: Not used: low selectivity, wrong column order, or functions wrapping the column.
B-tree index.example: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
B-tree index.integration: 1) Default to B-tree. 2) Match ORDER BY. 3) Watch bloat. 4) Prefer CONCURRENTLY.

BRIN index.summary: BRIN stores min/max summaries per page range—tiny indexes for naturally ordered columns.
BRIN index.problem: It speeds scans on large append-only time-series when values correlate with physical order.
BRIN index.mechanics: Planner skips ranges whose summary cannot match. Poor correlation makes BRIN useless.
BRIN index.tradeoffs: B-tree wins for selective point lookups on unordered keys.
BRIN index.troubleshoot: No speedup: check correlation; consider partitioning.
BRIN index.example: CREATE INDEX ON events USING brin (created_at);
BRIN index.integration: 1) Use on big time-ordered tables. 2) Verify correlation. 3) Pair with partitions. 4) Benchmark.

GIN index.summary: GIN inverted indexes elements inside arrays, jsonb, and full-text documents.
GIN index.problem: It makes containment and text-search queries practical.
GIN index.mechanics: Each component maps to rows containing it. Writes cost more than B-tree; tune pending lists.
GIN index.tradeoffs: Extracted B-tree on a generated column can replace GIN for single-field access.
GIN index.troubleshoot: Slow writes under heavy GIN updates—batch loads or reconsider design.
GIN index.example:
CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (body jsonb_path_ops);
SELECT * FROM docs WHERE body @> '{"status":"open"}';
GIN index.integration: 1) GIN for jsonb/array search. 2) jsonb_path_ops for @>-only. 3) Watch write latency. 4) EXPLAIN.

composite index.summary: A composite index covers multiple columns in order for multi-predicate filters and some sorts.
composite index.problem: It matches combined WHERE clauses better than disjoint single-column indexes.
composite index.mechanics: Put equality columns first, range last. (a,b) helps a and a+b, not b alone.
composite index.tradeoffs: Too-wide composites waste space; separate indexes may fit disjoint patterns better.
composite index.troubleshoot: Unused: order doesn't match query—EXPLAIN to confirm.
composite index.integration: 1) Mine top queries. 2) Design composites. 3) Drop redundant singles. 4) Validate with EXPLAIN.

covering/index-only scan.summary: A covering index includes all needed columns so Postgres can use an index-only scan.
covering/index-only scan.problem: It avoids heap fetches when the visibility map marks pages all-visible.
covering/index-only scan.mechanics: Planner picks index-only when index has required cols and VM allows. INCLUDE adds payload columns.
covering/index-only scan.tradeoffs: Wide covering indexes cost writes. Heap fetches remain if VM is stale.
covering/index-only scan.troubleshoot: High heap fetches: VACUUM to refresh visibility map.
covering/index-only scan.example:
CREATE INDEX ON users (email) INCLUDE (id, name);
EXPLAIN SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = 'a@b.com';
covering/index-only scan.integration: 1) Cover hot reads. 2) Use INCLUDE. 3) Keep VACUUM healthy. 4) Measure index size.

partial index.summary: A partial index indexes only rows matching a predicate (e.g., active rows).
partial index.problem: It shrinks indexes and speeds queries that share that predicate.
partial index.mechanics: CREATE INDEX … WHERE status='open'. Queries need compatible predicates for use.
partial index.tradeoffs: If queries need all rows, partial won't help those paths.
partial index.troubleshoot: Not used: query predicate not implied by index predicate.
partial index.example: CREATE INDEX ON tickets (priority) WHERE status = 'open';
partial index.integration: 1) Find skewed filters. 2) Partial-index hot subset. 3) Align query WHERE. 4) Monitor size.

EXPLAIN.summary: EXPLAIN shows the planner’s plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes and adds actual timings/rows.
EXPLAIN.problem: It is the primary tool for diagnosing slow SQL.
EXPLAIN.mechanics: Read inner-out: scans, joins, sorts. Compare estimated vs actual rows—bad stats cause bad plans.
EXPLAIN.tradeoffs: ANALYZE runs the query—wrap writes in a transaction you roll back if needed.
EXPLAIN.example: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
EXPLAIN.integration: 1) EXPLAIN slow SQL. 2) Fix indexes/stats. 3) Re-measure. 4) Attach plans in PRs.

query planner.summary: The planner costs alternative plans using statistics and chooses the cheapest expected path.
query planner.problem: Accurate stats and useful indexes are required for good plans.
query planner.mechanics: Rewrite → generate paths → cost → pick minimum. Row estimates drive nested loop vs hash/merge joins.
query planner.tradeoffs: Prefer fixing stats/indexes over hints (limited in Postgres).
query planner.troubleshoot: Bad plans after bulk load: ANALYZE; check work_mem for sorts/hashes.
query planner.integration: 1) Healthy autoanalyze. 2) Extended stats when correlated. 3) Tune work_mem. 4) Review after upgrades.

statistics/analyze.summary: ANALYZE collects histograms and most-common values so the planner estimates selectivities.
statistics/analyze.problem: Stale stats cause catastrophic plan choices.
statistics/analyze.mechanics: ANALYZE samples the table; autovacuum triggers autoanalyze after enough modifications.
statistics/analyze.tradeoffs: Override n_distinct for hard skew; create extended stats for correlated columns.
statistics/analyze.troubleshoot: Sudden plan flips: run ANALYZE; check last_analyze.
statistics/analyze.example:
ANALYZE VERBOSE orders;
SELECT last_analyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname='orders';
statistics/analyze.integration: 1) Keep autovacuum on. 2) ANALYZE after big loads. 3) Extended stats as needed. 4) Watch plan flips.

sequential scan.summary: A sequential scan reads the heap entirely—best for large fractions of a table or tiny tables.
sequential scan.problem: On selective filters it usually signals a missing or unusable index.
sequential scan.mechanics: Planner chooses seq scan when estimated filtered fraction is high or index cost is worse.
sequential scan.tradeoffs: Forcing an index can hurt—measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
sequential scan.troubleshoot: Unexpected seq scan: cast/function on column or stale stats.
sequential scan.example: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE type = 'x';
sequential scan.integration: 1) Check selectivity. 2) Add index if selective. 3) Avoid wrapping columns. 4) Re-ANALYZE.

VACUUM.summary: VACUUM reclaims dead tuple space from MVCC and updates the visibility map; VACUUM ANALYZE also refreshes stats.
VACUUM.problem: Without vacuum, tables bloat and performance collapses.
VACUUM.mechanics: Regular VACUUM reclaims in-place without exclusive lock; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table (heavy).
VACUUM.tradeoffs: Prefer tuning autovacuum over routine VACUUM FULL.
VACUUM.troubleshoot: Wraparound warnings: vacuum more aggressively; find long transactions.
VACUUM.integration: 1) Autovacuum adequately. 2) Monitor dead tuples/bloat. 3) Avoid idle-in-transaction. 4) Alert on xid age.

autovacuum.summary: Autovacuum launches workers that VACUUM/ANALYZE tables based on dead-tuple thresholds and xid age.
autovacuum.problem: It is required for healthy MVCC under continuous writes.
autovacuum.mechanics: Workers pick dirty tables; wraparound vacuums are forced when xid age is high.
autovacuum.tradeoffs: Hot tables often need lower scale_factor overrides.
autovacuum.troubleshoot: Lagging cleanup: raise workers or fix long-running transactions blocking vacuum.
autovacuum.example: SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 20;
autovacuum.integration: 1) Ensure enabled. 2) Tune busy tables. 3) Kill idle-in-transaction. 4) Dashboard dead tuples.

MVCC.summary: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so readers and writers rarely block each other.
MVCC.problem: It underpins Postgres concurrency and creates dead tuples that must be vacuumed.
MVCC.mechanics: Updates insert new versions; snapshots decide visibility; old versions become dead until VACUUM.
MVCC.tradeoffs: Long transactions delay cleanup and inflate bloat.
MVCC.troubleshoot: Bloat + replication lag: find old snapshots in pg_stat_activity.
MVCC.example: SELECT pid, state, xact_start, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state <> 'idle';
MVCC.integration: 1) Short transactions. 2) Monitor bloat. 3) Tune autovacuum. 4) Avoid idle-in-transaction sessions.

ACID.summary: ACID means Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability—the classic transaction guarantees.
ACID.problem: They keep multi-statement changes correct under concurrency and crashes.
ACID.mechanics: BEGIN…COMMIT applies all or nothing; isolation controls concurrent visibility; WAL fsync makes commits durable.
ACID.tradeoffs: Stronger isolation reduces anomalies but raises aborts/latency.
ACID.troubleshoot: Lost updates: raise isolation or use row locks/version columns.
ACID.integration: 1) Wrap multi-row invariants in transactions. 2) Choose isolation deliberately. 3) Keep txns short. 4) Test crash safety.

READ COMMITTED.summary: READ COMMITTED is Postgres’s default isolation: each statement sees only data committed before it began.
READ COMMITTED.problem: It prevents dirty reads while remaining cheap for many OLTP apps.
READ COMMITTED.mechanics: Each statement takes a new snapshot. Concurrent commits can change rows between statements in one transaction.
READ COMMITTED.tradeoffs: REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE for stronger guarantees at abort cost.
READ COMMITTED.troubleshoot: Lost updates under RC: use SELECT FOR UPDATE or version checks.
READ COMMITTED.example:
SHOW transaction_isolation;
-- read committed by default
READ COMMITTED.integration: 1) Know default is RC. 2) Escalate isolation for critical flows. 3) Add constraints. 4) Test concurrency.

SERIALIZABLE.summary: SERIALIZABLE isolation makes concurrent transactions behave as if executed one-at-a-time (SSI in Postgres).
SERIALIZABLE.problem: It prevents serialization anomalies that weaker levels allow.
SERIALIZABLE.mechanics: Postgres detects dangerous dependency cycles and aborts with 40001; apps must retry transactions.
SERIALIZABLE.tradeoffs: Higher abort rates under contention—keep transactions short.
SERIALIZABLE.troubleshoot: Frequent 40001: reduce txn scope or redesign hot spots.
SERIALIZABLE.example: -- SQLSTATE 40001: serialize retry loop in app
SERIALIZABLE.integration: 1) Enable for anomaly-sensitive paths. 2) Implement retry. 3) Keep txns tiny. 4) Monitor abort rates.

deadlock.summary: A deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting on each other’s locks; Postgres aborts one victim.
deadlock.problem: It freezes progress until the engine breaks the cycle.
deadlock.mechanics: Acquire locks in consistent order; keep transactions short; retry aborted victims idempotently.
deadlock.tradeoffs: Coarse locks reduce deadlock chance but hurt concurrency.
deadlock.troubleshoot: Logs show deadlock detail—reorder updates to match a global order.
deadlock.integration: 1) Stable lock ordering. 2) Short txns. 3) Retry on 40P01. 4) Alert on deadlock rate.

optimistic concurrency.summary: Optimistic concurrency detects write conflicts with version columns/ETags instead of holding long locks.
optimistic concurrency.problem: It scales when conflicts are rare.
optimistic concurrency.mechanics: Read row+version; write UPDATE … WHERE id=? AND version=?; if 0 rows, conflict—reload/retry.
optimistic concurrency.tradeoffs: High conflict rates need pessimistic locking or queuing.
optimistic concurrency.example: UPDATE docs SET body=$1, version=version+1 WHERE id=$2 AND version=$3;
optimistic concurrency.integration: 1) Add version columns. 2) Enforce in UPDATEs. 3) Return 409 to clients. 4) Retry policy.

WAL/PITR.summary: WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records changes before data files; PITR replays WAL to restore to a chosen time.
WAL/PITR.problem: It provides durability and continuous recovery beyond nightly dumps.
WAL/PITR.mechanics: Commit flushes WAL; base backup + archived WAL enables restore to timestamp/LSN.
WAL/PITR.tradeoffs: Logical dumps lack fine PITR. Synchronous commit trades latency for durability.
WAL/PITR.troubleshoot: Gap in WAL archive breaks PITR—monitor archive success.
WAL/PITR.integration: 1) Enable WAL archiving. 2) Regular base backups. 3) Test PITR. 4) Alert on archive failures.

logical backup.summary: Logical backups export SQL/objects (pg_dump) rather than copying data files.
logical backup.problem: They are portable across versions and good for selective restores.
logical backup.mechanics: pg_dump reads tables and writes archives; restore replays. Physical backups+WAL are better for huge DBs/PITR.
logical backup.tradeoffs: Logical restores are slower at scale; combine strategies.
logical backup.troubleshoot: Failed restore: version mismatches or missing roles—dump globals too.
logical backup.example:
pg_dump -Fc -f app.dump appdb
pg_restore -d appdb app.dump
logical backup.integration: 1) Schedule dumps. 2) Store offsite. 3) Test restore. 4) Also keep physical backups for large prod.

streaming replication.summary: Streaming replication ships WAL from primary to standbys for HA and read scaling.
streaming replication.problem: Standbys apply WAL continuously and can be promoted on failure.
streaming replication.mechanics: Standby connects, streams WAL, replays. Sync wait for flush ACK; async acknowledges later (possible data loss).
streaming replication.tradeoffs: Async is common; sync for zero-loss RPO at latency cost.
streaming replication.troubleshoot: Lag growth: network/disk or long queries on standby. Monitor replay_lag.
streaming replication.example: SELECT client_addr, state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;
streaming replication.integration: 1) Deploy ≥1 standby. 2) Monitor lag. 3) Rehearse promotion. 4) Choose sync intentionally.

replication.summary: Replication copies data to other nodes for HA, locality, or read scale (physical or logical).
replication.problem: It reduces downtime and can offload reads—but is not a backup by itself.
replication.mechanics: Primary accepts writes; replicas apply changes. Failover promotes a replica; fencing prevents split-brain.
replication.tradeoffs: Replicas don't protect against bad DELETEs—still need backups. Multi-primary is harder.
replication.troubleshoot: Lagging replica serving stale reads: route carefully; alert on lag.
replication.integration: 1) Define HA topology. 2) Monitor lag. 3) Backup still required. 4) Document failover.

failover.summary: Failover promotes a standby to primary when the old primary fails, restoring write availability.
failover.problem: It is the HA mechanism for RTO targets.
failover.mechanics: Detect failure; promote standby; repoint clients (DNS/VIP/proxy); fence old primary. Async replication may lose last commits.
failover.tradeoffs: Automatic failover can misfire—use consensus/lease systems carefully.
failover.troubleshoot: Split-brain: two primaries—require fencing. Test regularly.
failover.example: # patroni/repmgr/rds multi-AZ conceptual promote + endpoint flip
failover.integration: 1) Automate with fencing. 2) Client retry/backoff. 3) Game-day failovers. 4) Measure RTO/RPO.

PostgreSQL.summary: PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database with strong SQL, MVCC, extensibility, and reliability.
PostgreSQL.problem: It is a default choice for transactional systems needing integrity and rich queries.
PostgreSQL.mechanics: Clients speak SQL over the Postgres protocol; backends execute plans; WAL ensures durability.
PostgreSQL.tradeoffs: Managed services reduce ops. Not ideal as a sole analytics warehouse at extreme scale without care.
PostgreSQL.troubleshoot: Connection storms: use pooling. Slow queries: EXPLAIN + indexes.
PostgreSQL.integration: 1) Run managed Postgres if possible. 2) Migrations as code. 3) Pool connections. 4) Observe slow queries.

PostgreSQL process model.summary: Postgres uses a multi-process model: postmaster + one backend process per connection, plus workers (autovacuum, WAL writer).
PostgreSQL process model.problem: It isolates crashes per backend but makes connections relatively heavy.
PostgreSQL process model.mechanics: Each client connection forks/starts a backend attached to shared memory. Poolers multiplex app threads onto fewer connections.
PostgreSQL process model.tradeoffs: Thread-per-connection DBs differ. Too many connections exhaust memory—PgBouncer/ODS pool.
PostgreSQL process model.troubleshoot: Memory pressure with high conn count: lower max_connections and pool.
PostgreSQL process model.example:
SHOW max_connections;
SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;
PostgreSQL process model.integration: 1) Add a pooler. 2) Cap app pool sizes. 3) Monitor connection counts. 4) Separate pools per workload.

JSONB.summary: JSONB is Postgres’s binary JSON type supporting indexing and efficient operators for semi-structured data.
JSONB.problem: It stores flexible attributes without a separate document database.
JSONB.mechanics: Store jsonb; query with ->/->>/@>; index with GIN; promote hot keys to columns when stable.
JSONB.tradeoffs: Pure relational columns are clearer for core fields. Huge documents can bloat rows.
JSONB.troubleshoot: Slow jsonb filters: missing GIN or high-selectivity needs extracted columns.
JSONB.example:
CREATE TABLE events (id bigserial, body jsonb);
CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin (body jsonb_path_ops);
JSONB.integration: 1) Use jsonb for sparse attrs. 2) GIN for search. 3) Promote hot paths to columns. 4) Constrain shape in app.

row-level security.summary: Row-level security (RLS) filters which rows a role can see/modify via policies on tables.
row-level security.problem: It enforces tenancy in the database, not only in app code.
row-level security.mechanics: ENABLE RLS; CREATE POLICY using expressions like tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::uuid. Table owners bypass unless FORCE.
row-level security.tradeoffs: App bugs can still set wrong session vars—combine with careful auth. Policies add planning complexity.
row-level security.troubleshoot: Seeing all rows: RLS off or owner bypass—FORCE RLS and test as non-owner.
row-level security.example:
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_iso ON orders USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant')::uuid);
row-level security.integration: 1) Enable RLS on tenant tables. 2) Set session vars per request. 3) FORCE RLS. 4) Test with non-owner roles.

schema migration.summary: Schema migrations version database structure changes as ordered scripts applied by a tool (Flyway, Liquibase, golang-migrate).
schema migration.problem: They keep environments reproducible and reviewable.
schema migration.mechanics: Add forward migrations; deploy expand first (compatible); switch app; contract later. Avoid long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks.
schema migration.tradeoffs: Down migrations are often unsafe in prod—prefer forward fixes.
schema migration.troubleshoot: Stuck migration: lock wait—check pg_locks; use CONCURRENTLY for indexes.
schema migration.example:
-- 0014_add_orders_status.sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new';
schema migration.integration: 1) Migrations in Git/CI. 2) Expand/contract. 3) CONCURRENTLY for indexes. 4) Gate deploys on migrate success.

partitioning.summary: Partitioning splits a logical table into child partitions (range/list/hash) for manageability and pruning.
partitioning.problem: It speeds queries that prune partitions and eases dropping old data.
partitioning.mechanics: Declare PARTITION BY; insert routes to children; planner prunes irrelevant partitions. Detach/drop old ranges cheaply.
partitioning.tradeoffs: Wrong key prevents pruning. Too many partitions add planning overhead.
partitioning.troubleshoot: No pruning: predicate not on partition key or non-immutable expression.
partitioning.example: CREATE TABLE events (ts timestamptz, payload jsonb) PARTITION BY RANGE (ts);
partitioning.integration: 1) Choose key from query filters. 2) Automate creating partitions. 3) Drop old ones. 4) Verify pruning in EXPLAIN.

primary key.summary: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and implies NOT NULL + UNIQUE (usually indexed).
primary key.problem: It anchors foreign keys and ORM identity.
primary key.mechanics: DECLARE PRIMARY KEY; Postgres builds a unique index. Prefer stable opaque surrogates (bigint/uuid) for mutable natural keys.
primary key.tradeoffs: Natural keys change and cascade painfully. UUIDs trade locality for global uniqueness.
primary key.troubleshoot: Duplicate insert errors: constraint working—handle conflicts (UPSERT).
primary key.example: CREATE TABLE users (id biggenerated always as identity PRIMARY KEY, email text UNIQUE);
primary key.integration: 1) PK every table. 2) Prefer stable surrogates. 3) Index FKs referencing it. 4) Document allocation strategy.

foreign key.summary: A foreign key enforces that referenced parent rows exist, preserving relational integrity.
foreign key.problem: It prevents orphan child rows at the database layer.
foreign key.mechanics: INSERT/UPDATE child checks parent; DELETE parent restricted or cascades per action. Index FK columns for joins/deletes.
foreign key.tradeoffs: App-only integrity is fragile. Cascades can surprise—prefer explicit deletes sometimes.
foreign key.troubleshoot: Delete parent blocked: existing children. Check constraint violations in logs.
foreign key.example: ALTER TABLE orders ADD FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id);
foreign key.integration: 1) Add FKs for critical relations. 2) Index FK columns. 3) Choose delete actions carefully. 4) Test cascades.

1NF/2NF/3NF.summary: Normal forms (1NF/2NF/3NF) reduce redundancy via atomic columns and dependency rules on keys.
1NF/2NF/3NF.problem: They prevent update anomalies in OLTP schemas.
1NF/2NF/3NF.mechanics: Identify keys and FDs; decompose until non-key attributes depend only on keys. Denormalize later for read performance with clear sync.
1NF/2NF/3NF.tradeoffs: Warehouses often denormalize. Over-normalization can force heavy joins.
1NF/2NF/3NF.troubleshoot: Anomalies when same fact stored twice—normalize or add strict sync.
1NF/2NF/3NF.example: -- customers(id, city); orders(id, customer_id) instead of repeating city per order
1NF/2NF/3NF.integration: 1) Model FDs. 2) Normalize OLTP. 3) Denormalize with metrics. 4) Document derived data.

normalization.summary: Normalization structures relational schemas to store each fact once and avoid update anomalies.
normalization.problem: It keeps transactional data consistent as application writes evolve.
normalization.mechanics: Decompose tables per normal forms; use joins/views for combined reads.
normalization.troubleshoot: Update bugs fixing many tables: under-normalized design.
normalization.example: -- split repeating groups into child tables
normalization.integration: 1) Start normalized. 2) Measure join cost. 3) Denormalize with jobs/triggers if needed. 4) Add tests for invariants.

relational model.summary: The relational model represents data as relations (tables) queried via relational algebra/SQL.
relational model.problem: It provides a precise foundation for integrity and declarative querying.
relational model.mechanics: Define schemas; query declaratively; engine chooses plans. Integrity via keys/FKs/CHECK.
relational model.tradeoffs: Document models fit flexible hierarchies; relational shines for interlocking invariants.
relational model.troubleshoot: Unexpected fanout: join cardinality—validate with COUNTs.
relational model.example: SELECT u.email, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id=u.id;
relational model.integration: 1) Model entities/keys. 2) Constraints in DB. 3) Index join columns. 4) EXPLAIN heavy queries.

INNER JOIN.summary: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matches in both tables on the join predicate.
INNER JOIN.problem: It is the default way to combine related relational data.
INNER JOIN.mechanics: Planner may use nested loop/hash/merge. Unmatched rows are excluded (unlike LEFT JOIN).
INNER JOIN.tradeoffs: LEFT JOIN when you must keep unmatched left rows. Accidental CROSS JOIN explodes rows.
INNER JOIN.troubleshoot: Row explosion: many-to-many without aggregation—check distinct counts.
INNER JOIN.example: SELECT u.id, o.id FROM users u INNER JOIN orders o ON o.user_id=u.id;
INNER JOIN.integration: 1) Prefer SQL joins over app loops. 2) Index join keys. 3) EXPLAIN large joins. 4) Test unmatched cases with outer joins when needed.

GROUP BY.summary: GROUP BY aggregates rows sharing key expressions with COUNT/SUM/AVG/etc.
GROUP BY.problem: It powers reporting and rollups in SQL.
GROUP BY.mechanics: Filter with WHERE pre-aggregate; HAVING filters groups. SELECT list must be grouped or aggregated (Postgres allows PK FD exceptions).
GROUP BY.tradeoffs: Window functions for per-row analytics without collapsing groups.
GROUP BY.troubleshoot: Wrong totals: join fanout before aggregate—aggregate in subquery first.
GROUP BY.example: SELECT user_id, SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING SUM(total) > 100;
GROUP BY.integration: 1) Index group keys when selective. 2) Pre-aggregate carefully. 3) Prefer windows when keeping detail. 4) Test null groups.

UNION.summary: UNION combines result sets; UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them (faster).
UNION.problem: It merges homogeneous outputs from different queries.
UNION.mechanics: Each branch projects compatible columns; UNION sorts/hashes to dedupe; ALL concatenates.
UNION.troubleshoot: Slow UNION: dedup—switch to ALL or push filters.
UNION.example: SELECT id FROM a UNION ALL SELECT id FROM b;
UNION.integration: 1) Match schemas. 2) Prefer UNION ALL. 3) Wrap ORDER BY outside. 4) EXPLAIN dedup cost.

subquery.summary: A subquery is a query nested in another SQL statement (FROM/WHERE/SELECT).
subquery.problem: It expresses multi-step logic without temp tables.
subquery.mechanics: Planner may decorrelate into joins. EXISTS often beats IN for large nullable sets. LATERAL allows referencing left-hand rows.
subquery.tradeoffs: CTEs can be optimization fences historically—understand version behavior.
subquery.troubleshoot: Slow IN lists: rewrite as JOIN/EXISTS.
subquery.example: SELECT * FROM users u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id=u.id);
subquery.integration: 1) Prefer EXISTS for existence. 2) EXPLAIN. 3) Use LATERAL for top-N per group. 4) Avoid correlated row-by-row when a join works.

correlated subquery.summary: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query and conceptually runs per outer row.
correlated subquery.problem: It expresses per-row dependent lookups but can be expensive if not decorrelated.
correlated subquery.mechanics: Write EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM … WHERE outer.id=…). Planner often turns it into a semi-join.
correlated subquery.tradeoffs: Joins/windows may be clearer/faster for aggregations per parent.
correlated subquery.troubleshoot: Nested loop explosion: missing index on inner predicate.
correlated subquery.example: SELECT u.* FROM users u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sessions s WHERE s.user_id=u.id AND s.active);
correlated subquery.integration: 1) Index inner keys. 2) Prefer EXISTS. 3) EXPLAIN for semi-joins. 4) Rewrite to joins when clearer.

window function.summary: Window functions compute values across related rows without collapsing the result set (OVER clause).
window function.problem: They enable rankings, running totals, and lead/lag analytics in one pass.
window function.mechanics: Each row stays; function sees a window frame. ROW_NUMBER for top-N per group patterns via subquery filter.
window function.tradeoffs: GROUP BY collapses; windows keep detail. Large sorts need memory—watch work_mem.
window function.troubleshoot: Wrong totals: frame defaults (RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING). Be explicit.
window function.example: SELECT user_id, total, SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at) AS running FROM orders;
window function.integration: 1) Use for rankings/running metrics. 2) Index partition/order keys. 3) Explicit frames. 4) EXPLAIN sorts.

ROW_NUMBER.summary: ROW_NUMBER() assigns unique ranks within a partition ordered by given keys.
ROW_NUMBER.problem: It is the standard tool for top-N-per-group queries.
ROW_NUMBER.mechanics: Wrap in subquery/CTE and filter WHERE rn <= N. Ties get different numbers (unlike RANK).
ROW_NUMBER.tradeoffs: RANK/DENSE_RANK for competition ranking with ties.
ROW_NUMBER.troubleshoot: Unstable order: add deterministic tiebreakers to ORDER BY.
ROW_NUMBER.integration: 1) Deterministic ORDER BY. 2) Filter rn. 3) Index (user_id, created_at). 4) Compare to DISTINCT ON in Postgres.

NULL semantics.summary: NULL means unknown/missing; comparisons with NULL yield UNKNOWN, so WHERE clauses need IS NULL / IS DISTINCT FROM.
NULL semantics.problem: Misunderstanding NULL causes wrong filters and broken UNIQUE behavior (multiple NULLs allowed in UNIQUE).
NULL semantics.mechanics: Use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL; prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN with nullable columns; COALESCE for defaults.
NULL semantics.tradeoffs: Empty string ≠ NULL. Constraints: NOT NULL when required.
NULL semantics.troubleshoot: Missing rows from NOT IN: NULL in the list—rewrite.
NULL semantics.example:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
SELECT * FROM t WHERE a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b;
NULL semantics.integration: 1) NOT NULL on required cols. 2) Ban NOT IN on nullable. 3) Document NULL meaning. 4) Test edge data.

view.summary: A view is a stored SELECT presented as a table; it encapsulates joins/filters for reuse.
view.problem: It simplifies queries and can restrict column exposure (with security_barrier/RLS care).
view.mechanics: CREATE VIEW; queries against it are rewritten/planned with the underlying SQL. Materialized views store results and need refresh.
view.tradeoffs: Complex views can hide expensive joins—inspect EXPLAIN. Prefer plain SQL functions carefully.
view.troubleshoot: Unexpected slowness: view expanded into heavy join graph.
view.example: CREATE VIEW open_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='open';
view.integration: 1) Encapsulate common joins. 2) EXPLAIN consumer queries. 3) Materialize expensive reports. 4) Version via migrations.

trigger.summary: A trigger runs a function on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events to enforce logic or maintain derived data.
trigger.problem: It centralizes invariants inside the database.
trigger.mechanics: CREATE TRIGGER executes function per event. Prefer constraints when they suffice; keep triggers simple and documented.
trigger.tradeoffs: Hidden write amplification surprises apps. Business logic in DB vs app is a trade-off.
trigger.troubleshoot: Infinite trigger loops: guard with WHEN or flags.
trigger.example:
CREATE FUNCTION … RETURNS trigger AS $$ BEGIN NEW.updated_at=now(); RETURN NEW; END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
CREATE TRIGGER … BEFORE UPDATE ON orders FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION …;
trigger.integration: 1) Prefer constraints. 2) Document triggers. 3) Keep them fast. 4) Test bulk updates.

function/procedure.summary: SQL functions/procedures encapsulate reusable server-side logic; procedures can manage transactions (in Postgres CALL).
function/procedure.problem: They move logic close to data for atomic multi-step operations.
function/procedure.mechanics: CREATE FUNCTION returns values; PROCEDURE can COMMIT/ROLLBACK in controlled ways. Mark volatility correctly for optimization.
function/procedure.tradeoffs: SECURITY DEFINER is powerful—avoid SQL injection via dynamic SQL; prefer app services for complex domains.
function/procedure.troubleshoot: Permission errors: ownership/SECURITY. Deadlocks inside long routines—keep short.
function/procedure.example: CREATE FUNCTION add(a int,b int) RETURNS int LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS $$ SELECT a+b; $$;
function/procedure.integration: 1) Use for tight data invariants. 2) Avoid dynamic SQL string concat. 3) Grant carefully. 4) Version in migrations.

N+1 queries.summary: N+1 queries fetch a list then run one query per row for related data, causing O(N) round-trips.
N+1 queries.problem: It destroys latency as lists grow.
N+1 queries.mechanics: Detect via query logs; fix with JOIN, select-in, or dataloader batching. Index foreign keys.
N+1 queries.tradeoffs: Over-fetching joins can also hurt—fetch what you need.
N+1 queries.troubleshoot: Dev fast/prod slow: classic N+1 under larger N—enable ORM query logging.
N+1 queries.example:
-- bad: for each user: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=?
-- good: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ANY(%s)
N+1 queries.integration: 1) Log SQL in staging. 2) Prefetch relations. 3) Add integration tests for query counts. 4) Index FKs.

slow query log.summary: A slow query log records statements exceeding a duration threshold for performance triage.
slow query log.problem: It finds real production offenders beyond guesswork.
slow query log.mechanics: Set threshold; aggregate with pg_stat_statements; EXPLAIN top offenders; fix indexes/SQL.
slow query log.tradeoffs: Logging everything is noisy/expensive—use thresholds + extensions.
slow query log.troubleshoot: Missing culprits: threshold too high or statements not logged (prep). Use pg_stat_statements.
slow query log.example:
ALTER SYSTEM SET log_min_duration_statement = 500; -- ms
SELECT query, mean_exec_time FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC LIMIT 20;
slow query log.integration: 1) Enable duration logging. 2) Install pg_stat_statements. 3) Weekly top-10 review. 4) Track improvements.

OLTP.summary: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems run many small read/write transactions with strong integrity needs.
OLTP.problem: They power apps like payments and order management.
OLTP.mechanics: Optimize for p99 latency of small statements; keep transactions short; use connection pooling.
OLTP.tradeoffs: Warehouses (OLAP) prefer columnar scans and denormalization. HTAP blends both carefully.
OLTP.troubleshoot: Analytical queries on OLTP primary: move to replicas/warehouse.
OLTP.example: -- typical OLTP: primary key lookup + small update in one txn
OLTP.integration: 1) Separate OLTP from heavy analytics. 2) Index point paths. 3) Pool conns. 4) Replica for reports.

CAP theorem.summary: CAP says in a network partition a distributed system must choose consistency or availability (plus partition tolerance reality).
CAP theorem.problem: It frames trade-offs for multi-node data systems—not a daily toggle for single-node Postgres.
CAP theorem.mechanics: During partitions, CP systems refuse divergent writes; AP systems stay up with potential divergence/conflict resolution.
CAP theorem.tradeoffs: PACELC adds latency vs consistency when not partitioned. Most app DBs are CP within a primary.
CAP theorem.troubleshoot: Don't misuse CAP as buzzword—state concrete failure modes (split-brain, stale reads).
CAP theorem.example: # example: Raft consensus elects one primary (CP leaning) vs Dynamo-style quorum/repair (AP leaning)
CAP theorem.integration: 1) State required consistency. 2) Pick topology accordingly. 3) Document partition behavior. 4) Test failure modes.

connection pool.summary: A connection pool reuses a limited set of DB connections across many app requests/threads.
connection pool.problem: It prevents connection storms against process-per-connection servers like Postgres.
connection pool.mechanics: App or proxy maintains N open connections; requests checkout/return. Size ≈ (cores × (1 + wait/service)) carefully; often tens not hundreds.
connection pool.tradeoffs: Pool too large still overwhelms DB. Transaction pooling limits session features (temp tables, prepared).
connection pool.troubleshoot: Timeouts under load: pool exhausted—raise carefully or reduce query time.
connection pool.example: # PgBouncer transaction pooling in front of Postgres
connection pool.integration: 1) Add pooler. 2) Cap app pools. 3) Monitor wait/checkout. 4) Prefer transaction mode carefully.

cache-aside.summary: Cache-aside (lazy loading) makes the app read cache first, load from DB on miss, then populate cache.
cache-aside.problem: It is the common pattern for Redis in front of OLTP reads.
cache-aside.mechanics: On write, update DB then delete/update cache key. Use TTL as safety net; singleflight on hot misses.
cache-aside.tradeoffs: Write-through simplifies reads but complicates writes. Stale windows are explicit trade-offs.
cache-aside.troubleshoot: Stampede after expiry: lock/probabilistic early expire.
cache-aside.integration: 1) Identify hot keys. 2) Implement get/set/invalidate. 3) Cap TTL. 4) Measure hit rate.

Redis.summary: Redis is an in-memory data structure server used for caches, sessions, locks, rate limits, and queues.
Redis.problem: It provides microsecond operations and rich types beyond simple KV.
Redis.mechanics: Clients run commands (GET/SET/HSET/…). Persistence (RDB/AOF) is optional; treat as ephemeral unless configured and tested.
Redis.tradeoffs: Not a primary durable DB for critical truth without care. Memory cost dominates.
Redis.troubleshoot: Evictions/OOM: set maxmemory policies; split hot keys.
Redis.example:
redis-cli SET session:1 '{"uid":42}' EX 3600
redis-cli GET session:1
Redis.integration: 1) Use for cache/session/limits. 2) Set maxmemory+policy. 3) Decide persistence needs. 4) Monitor hit/evict.

Redis string.summary: Redis strings store bytes/text values—and can act as counters/bitmaps—with optional TTL.
Redis string.problem: They are the basic building block for cache entries and session blobs.
Redis string.mechanics: SET key value EX seconds; GET retrieves; INCR atomically increments integer strings.
Redis string.tradeoffs: Huge values hurt; prefer hashes for many fields. JSON blobs are fine if sized reasonably.
Redis string.troubleshoot: Unexpected nil: expiry or eviction. Check TTL.
Redis string.integration: 1) Standardize key names. 2) Always consider TTL. 3) Cap value size. 4) Use INCR for counters.

TTL.summary: TTL (time-to-live) expires keys automatically after a duration—central to cache correctness and memory control.
TTL.problem: It bounds staleness and prevents unbounded growth.
TTL.mechanics: SET with EX or EXPIRE; Redis removes lazily on access and periodically samples. Add jitter to avoid stampedes.
TTL.tradeoffs: TTL too long serves stale; too short thunders origin.
TTL.troubleshoot: Keys never die: missing TTL or persistence reload without expiry—audit object idle times.
TTL.example:
SET config:x v EX 60
TTL config:x
TTL.integration: 1) Default TTLs by data class. 2) Jitter hot keys. 3) Alert on no-TTL growth. 4) Document staleness SLOs.

set.summary: A Redis set is an unordered unique string collection supporting SADD/SMEMBERS/sinter operations.
set.problem: It models tags, unique visitors, and membership tests.
set.mechanics: SADD inserts; SISMEMBER tests; SUNION/SINTER combine. Sorted sets add scores for rankings.
set.tradeoffs: Large SMEMBERS can block—use SSCAN. For rankings use ZSET.
set.troubleshoot: Blocking ops on huge sets: scan iteratively.
set.example:
SADD user:42:tags sports music
SISMEMBER user:42:tags sports
set.integration: 1) Use sets for membership. 2) SSCAN for large. 3) Expire key. 4) Prefer ZSET when order/score needed.

stream.summary: Redis streams are append-only log structures with consumer groups for messaging patterns.
stream.problem: They provide lightweight queue/eventing inside Redis.
stream.mechanics: Producers XADD entries; consumers in groups claim pending entries and XACK. Unlike Kafka, retention/ops differ.
stream.tradeoffs: For large durable event buses, Kafka may fit better. Redis streams excel for simpler workloads.
stream.troubleshoot: Growing lag: scale consumers or fix poison messages (XPENDING).
stream.example:
XADD orders * item_id 123
XREADGROUP GROUP g c COUNT 10 STREAMS orders >
stream.integration: 1) Define stream keys. 2) Consumer groups. 3) Idempotent handlers. 4) Monitor lag/pending.

persistence RDB.summary: RDB persistence snapshots Redis memory to disk periodically for restart recovery.
persistence RDB.problem: It trades durability windows for simpler/faster persistence than full AOF.
persistence RDB.mechanics: BGSAVE forks and writes .rdb; on restart Redis loads snapshot. Changes since last save can be lost.
persistence RDB.tradeoffs: AOF fsync policies give stronger durability at cost. Many cache use-cases disable persistence.
persistence RDB.troubleshoot: Long forks stall under memory pressure—monitor COW and use replicas for bgsave offload.
persistence RDB.integration: 1) Decide if Redis is durable. 2) Configure RDB/AOF. 3) Test restart restore. 4) Monitor save failures.

hot key.summary: A hot key receives disproportionate traffic, concentrating CPU/network on one Redis shard/key.
hot key.problem: It creates latency spikes and uneven cluster load.
hot key.mechanics: Detect via shard CPU and commandstats; mitigate with in-process cache, split keys, or read replicas; coalesce identical gets.
hot key.tradeoffs: Clustering doesn't help if one key is the hotspot—must split logically.
hot key.troubleshoot: One key dominates MONITOR/hotstats—add local L1 cache with short TTL.
hot key.integration: 1) Detect skew. 2) L1 cache. 3) Split keys. 4) Coalesce stampedes.

distributed lock.summary: A distributed lock coordinates mutual exclusion across processes using Redis/etcd with TTLs.
distributed lock.problem: It prevents duplicate workers from running the same critical section.
distributed lock.mechanics: SET lock:name token NX EX 30; do work; delete only if token matches. Prefer fencing tokens for correctness under pauses.
distributed lock.tradeoffs: Locks aren't enough for correctness without fencing in all failure modes. DB constraints often simpler.
distributed lock.troubleshoot: Dead lock holders: TTL expiry; ensure work is idempotent.
distributed lock.example:
SET lock:job:42 token NX EX 30
# release: if GET==token then DEL
distributed lock.integration: 1) Prefer DB uniqueness when possible. 2) TTL all locks. 3) Compare-and-del token. 4) Make work idempotent.

MongoDB index.summary: MongoDB indexes (B-tree-like) speed queries/sorts on document fields, including compound and multikey indexes.
MongoDB index.mechanics: createIndex on fields; explain() shows IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN. Equality-Sort-Range field order for compounds.
MongoDB index.tradeoffs: Too many indexes hurt writes. Wildcards carefully for flexible schemas.
MongoDB index.troubleshoot: COLLSCAN in explain: add/repair index; check types/selectivity.
MongoDB index.example:
db.orders.createIndex({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 })
db.orders.find({ userId: 42 }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).explain('executionStats')
MongoDB index.integration: 1) Index common filters/sorts. 2) Follow ESR. 3) Drop unused. 4) explain in review.

document embedding.summary: Embedding stores related subdocuments inside a parent document instead of referencing another collection.
document embedding.problem: It makes common reads a single fetch when data is tightly bounded.
document embedding.mechanics: Embed when data is accessed together and bounded; reference when shared/large/many-to-many. Update patterns decide.
document embedding.tradeoffs: Unbounded arrays are an anti-pattern. Transactions across docs cost more.
document embedding.troubleshoot: Huge documents/slow updates: extract to references.
document embedding.example:
// embed addresses inside user when few and owned
{ _id, email, addresses: [{city, zip}] }
document embedding.integration: 1) Model access patterns first. 2) Bound arrays. 3) Reference shared entities. 4) Enforce size checks.

aggregation pipeline.summary: MongoDB aggregation pipelines transform documents through ordered stages ($match, $group, $lookup, …).
aggregation pipeline.problem: They express analytics and reshaping without pulling raw data to the app.
aggregation pipeline.mechanics: Place $match/$project early to cut data; use indexes for $match/$sort; allowDiskUse for large sorts carefully.
aggregation pipeline.tradeoffs: SQL engines may be better for heavy relational analytics. $lookup is not a free join.
aggregation pipeline.troubleshoot: OOM/slow: reduce working set; index; simplify groups.
aggregation pipeline.integration: 1) $match first. 2) Index match/sort fields. 3) Limit stages. 4) Explain pipelines.

multi-document transaction.summary: MongoDB multi-document transactions provide ACID across documents/collections on replica sets/sharded clusters.
multi-document transaction.problem: They allow relational-style invariants when embedding cannot express them.
multi-document transaction.mechanics: Start session/transaction; perform ops; commit. Keep short; handle TransientTransactionError retries.
multi-document transaction.tradeoffs: Prefer single-document atomicity when possible—it's cheaper and simpler.
multi-document transaction.troubleshoot: Frequent aborts: contention—narrow scope or remodel.
multi-document transaction.example:
session = client.start_session()
with session.start_transaction():
    coll.update_one({'_id':1},{'$inc':{'n':1}}, session=session)
    session.commit_transaction()
multi-document transaction.integration: 1) Default to single-doc atomicity. 2) Use multi-doc sparingly. 3) Retry transients. 4) Monitor abort rates.

replica set.summary: A MongoDB replica set is a primary plus secondaries replicating the oplog for HA and read preference options.
replica set.problem: It provides automatic failover for the database tier.
replica set.mechanics: Writes go to primary; secondaries replicate; elections promote on failure. Choose writeConcern/readConcern deliberately.
replica set.tradeoffs: Secondary reads can be stale. Sharded clusters build on replica sets per shard.
replica set.troubleshoot: Lagging secondary: check oplog window and load. Test failover.
replica set.integration: 1) Prod as replica set. 2) Tune concerns. 3) Monitor lag. 4) Rehearse failover.

role.summary: Database roles bundle privileges granted to users (Postgres ROLEs / Mongo roles).
role.problem: They implement least privilege for apps and humans.
role.mechanics: Create group roles with grants; assign users/app roles. Avoid superuser for apps.
role.tradeoffs: Too-broad grants increase breach impact. Migrate privileges with schema.
role.troubleshoot: Permission denied: missing GRANT. Audit \du / roles.
role.example:
CREATE ROLE app_rw LOGIN PASSWORD '…';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO app_rw;
role.integration: 1) Role per app. 2) Minimal grants. 3) No superuser apps. 4) Review quarterly.

DB-B-0010.summary: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps all left rows; RIGHT all right; FULL keeps either side with NULLs for gaps.
DB-B-0010.example: SELECT u.id, o.id FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id=u.id;
DB-B-0010.integration: 1) Choose join type from the question you’re asking. 2) Index join keys. 3) Test unmatched rows. 4) EXPLAIN large joins.
DB-B-0010.shortAnswer: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps all left rows; RIGHT all right; FULL keeps either side with NULLs for gaps.
DB-B-0010.answer: Join type decides which unmatched rows survive. Prefer INNER when both sides must exist; LEFT for optional relations.

DB-B-0011.summary: SELECT reads; INSERT adds rows; UPDATE modifies; DELETE removes—DML for relational tables.
DB-B-0011.example: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-1 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
DB-B-0011.integration: 1) Parameterize all SQL. 2) Transactional multi-writes. 3) Audit destructive deletes. 4) Add constraints.
DB-B-0011.shortAnswer: SELECT reads; INSERT adds rows; UPDATE modifies; DELETE removes—DML for relational tables.
DB-B-0011.answer: Wrap multi-step changes in transactions. Prefer soft-delete only with a clear policy.

DB-B-0012.summary: Common Redis types: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams—each fits different access patterns.
DB-B-0012.example: SADD tags:1 a b; ZADD leaderboard 100 alice; XADD events * type signup
DB-B-0012.integration: 1) Pick type by query. 2) TTL keys. 3) Cap memory. 4) Monitor hot keys.
DB-B-0012.shortAnswer: Common Redis types: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams—each fits different access patterns.
DB-B-0012.answer: Strings for blobs/counters; hashes for objects; lists for queues; sets for membership; zsets for rankings; streams for event logs.

DB-B-0013.summary: Primary key identifies rows; candidate keys are minimal unique sets; unique constraints enforce alternate keys; foreign keys reference parents.
DB-B-0013.example: email TEXT UNIQUE; id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY; user_id REFERENCES users(id)
DB-B-0013.integration: 1) Declare keys in schema. 2) Index FKs. 3) Prefer stable PKs. 4) Document natural vs surrogate keys.
DB-B-0013.shortAnswer: Primary key identifies rows; candidate keys are minimal unique sets; unique constraints enforce alternate keys; foreign keys reference parents.
DB-B-0013.answer: One primary key per table; multiple unique/candidate keys possible; FKs enforce relational integrity.

DB-B-0014.summary: Atomicity all-or-nothing; Consistency constraints hold; Isolation concurrency behavior; Durability committed data survives crashes.
DB-B-0014.integration: 1) Transactional invariants. 2) Choose isolation. 3) Short txns. 4) Backup/PITR still required.
DB-B-0014.shortAnswer: Atomicity all-or-nothing; Consistency constraints hold; Isolation concurrency behavior; Durability committed data survives crashes.
DB-B-0014.answer: Together they define correct transactions. Isolation level tunes the concurrency/anomaly trade-off.

DB-B-0015.summary: GROUP BY aggregates rows sharing a key with SUM/COUNT/AVG and filters groups via HAVING.
DB-B-0015.example: SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;
DB-B-0015.integration: 1) Index group keys when helpful. 2) Avoid join fanout before aggregate. 3) Test NULL groups. 4) EXPLAIN.
DB-B-0015.shortAnswer: GROUP BY aggregates rows sharing a key with SUM/COUNT/AVG and filters groups via HAVING.
DB-B-0015.answer: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters after.
